66.59 ounces of silver now buys one ounce of gold — the narrowest that ratio has been in four sessions of trading.

Kitco's live board this morning read gold at $4,415.20 and silver at $66.30, both re-read and checked against a second page before this desk's tape moved. Gold is up 0.97% on yesterday's mark. Silver is up 2.33% — more than double gold's move, and the fourth straight session it has out-run the metal. The ratio itself has fallen from 68.41 on 9 August to 67.84, to 67.49, to 66.59 this morning: 1.82 points taken out of gold's purchasing power over silver in three sessions, with today's step the largest of the four.

The practical number for anyone quoting metal across a counter isn't gold, it's silver. A workshop pricing stock off a sheet printed two days ago is already 4.5% behind. Platinum tells the opposite story: three public pages disagreed by nearly 2% this morning, and one was serving yesterday's number with yesterday's change still attached — this desk held its mark rather than take a fresh-looking figure it couldn't stand behind.

Signet just gave two of its jewellery chains to two very different résumés.

Jamie Cygielman becomes president of Zales and Banter on 24 August, arriving from Mattel, where she was global head of dolls after running American Girl and later widening into Barbie. She has never sold jewellery. Eight days earlier, Signet named Pam Cloud president of Blue Nile — more than 25 years at Tiffany and Co., most recently as chief merchandising officer.

Under Signet's Grow Brand Love strategy, four customer families each got a different read on what their problem is. Blue Nile's was treated as a merchandising problem: what's bought, at what margin. Zales and Banter's was treated as a brand problem: what the name means, and to whom. That's a bet that fashion-jewellery shoppers choose the sign before they choose the stone.

The metal doesn't care which theory is right. Gold reads $4,415.20 an ounce this morning, up 6.2% on a week ago, and Zales sells into exactly the price points with the least room to absorb that. A brand president can change what a chain means. She can't change what the metal costs.

July's one-carat diamond index read flat. Broken open by colour, it wasn't.

This paper led on 4 August with the one-carat polished index unchanged for the month — the first time in thirteen months it hadn't fallen. Rapaport's August Diamond Pulse now splits that flat line by colour: the best colours, D to F and G to J in IF-VVS and VS clarity, averaged a 0.1% gain. The cheapest colours, K to M, averaged 1.7% — seventeen times the move, on this desk's own division. K to M in VS clarity swung from a 0.1% loss in June to a 2.8% gain in July.

A flat index is an average, and averages hide the thing that moved. The one-carat headline was flat because a near-flat top and a rising bottom cancelled each other out inside it — and a jeweller quoting the single figure as evidence of a turn was reading the one number in the set that didn't turn.

This is the same shape this desk found in the size chart on 4 August, where 0.30-carat goods gained 1.6% and 0.50-carat goods 1.8% against a flat one-carat. The recovery is now running bottom-up on size and on colour. One caveat holds: it's one source, and that source owns the index. One month is composition. Two is a trend.
